source: Golomb rulers (Sidon sets): the lengths of optimal rulers are tabulated in OEIS A003022 and on the Wikipedia page "Golomb ruler"; the table of optimal rulers for 1 <= n <= 13 was found by exhaustive computer search by several authors (names and years cited from memory, not verified here). title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 55 — on a theme by Kaplansky: zero-divisor conjecture for torsion-free abelian groups
author: @Secousses
source: Origin of this statement: the abelian case of Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture, platform problem FCP.Kaplansky.zero_divisor_conjecture (Open), with G assumed commutative. The conjecture is attributed to Kaplansky; no page or theorem number is quoted here. The abelian case is an elementary consequence of the definitions together with Mathlib: a torsion-free abelian group A embeds in the Q-vector space Q (x) A, which is ordered, so A has the unique-sums property (Mathlib: UniqueSums.of_injective_addHom), and Mathlib proves that unique products over a domain give NoZeroDivisors for the monoid algebra. (Earlier drafts mentioned Passman 1977 ch. 13, Levi 1913 and Higman 1940; those references were not verified and are deliberately omitted.)

title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 57 — on a theme by Ellenberg and Gijswijt: cap sets in F_3^n have at most 2.756^n points for n at most 8
author: @Secousses
source: J. S. Ellenberg and D. Gijswijt, On large subsets of F_q^n with no three-term arithmetic progression, Annals of Mathematics 185 (2017), 339-343 (after E. Croot, V. F. Lev and P. P. Pach, Progression-free sets in Z_4^n are exponentially small, Annals of Mathematics 185 (2017), 331-337); journal volume and page numbers cited from memory, not re-checked. The line-counting bound |A| <= (3^n+1)/2 for a cap set in F_3^n is folklore (elementary: through a point of the cap, each of the (3^n-1)/2 lines through it contains at most one other point of the cap); no source is claimed for it. Origin of this statement: the range 1 <= n <= 8 of the platform theorem cap_set_bound (Open), whose conclusion and hypotheses it copies verbatim, with the extra hypothesis n <= 8; it is proved by the line-counting bound together with the arithmetic check that (3^n+1)/2 <= 2.756^n for n <= 8 (3281 <= 3328.4 at n = 8, while 9842 > 9173.0 at n = 9).

author: @Secousses
source: Origin of this statement: the abelian case of Kaplansky's idempotent conjecture, platform problem FCP.Kaplansky.idempotent_conjecture (Open), with G assumed commutative. The conjecture is attributed to Kaplansky; no page or theorem number is quoted here. The abelian case is an elementary consequence of the definitions together with Mathlib: a torsion-free abelian group has the unique-product property (it embeds in an ordered Q-vector space), so K[G] has no zero divisors, and a^2 = a gives a(a-1) = 0. title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 94 — on a theme by Wills: the lonely runner with seven runners, coprime speeds of small gcd-sum
author: @Secousses
source: Posed by Erwan Lefebvre (series Lefebvre's variations). Statement true by D. Rosenfeld, The lonely runner conjecture holds for eight runners (2025) (LRC(7)), together with the cases up to six moving runners (Barajas–Serra); it is the part of that theorem left after the reduction of N. Malikiosis, M. Santos, M. Schymura, Linear programming bounds / On the lonely runner conjecture (Theorem A: gcd-one vectors with sum of subset gcds above C(n+1,2)^(n-1) follow from LRC(n-1)). Citations from memory (no network). Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of `LonelyRunnerConjecture.rosenfeld_eight_runners` (LRC 7). Malikiosis–Santos–Schymura (Theorem A, platform theorem `LonelyRunnerConjecture.mss_finite_checking`) handles every gcd-one speed vector whose gcd-sum exceeds C(n+1,2)^(n-1) once LRC(n-1) is known; what is left is the finite range gcd-sum ≤ C(n+1,2)^(n-1). The file `lonely_runner_seven_small_gcd_sum_reduction.lean` derives `LonelyRunnerConjecture.rosenfeld_eight_runners` (LRC 7) from this statement, `mss_finite_checking` and `classical_small_cases` (for LRC 6); the Lean proof of the gcd-normalisation (divide by g = gcd S) and the case split is complete.

Larger kissing configurations in dimension 9 may be known; only the lower bound 306 is asserted. Origin: the open mission 'The Kissing Number Problem'.

source:

title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 120 — on a theme by Rosenfeld: the lonely runner with nine and ten runners, coprime speeds of small gcd-sum
author: @Secousses
source: Posed by Erwan Lefebvre (series Lefebvre's variations). Statement true by W. Trakulthongchai, The lonely runner conjecture holds for nine and ten runners (2025), given the preceding case (Rosenfeld 2025 for n=8; the n=9 instance uses n=8). It is the finite range left by N. Malikiosis, M. Santos, M. Schymura, Theorem A. Citations from memory (no network). Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of `LonelyRunnerConjecture.trakulthongchai_nine_ten` (LRC 8 ∧ LRC 9). Malikiosis–Santos–Schymura (Theorem A, platform theorem `LonelyRunnerConjecture.mss_finite_checking`) handles every gcd-one speed vector whose gcd-sum exceeds C(n+1,2)^(n-1) once LRC(n-1) is known; what is left is the finite range gcd-sum ≤ C(n+1,2)^(n-1). The file `lonely_runner_eight_nine_small_gcd_sum_reduction.lean` derives `LonelyRunnerConjecture.trakulthongchai_nine_ten` (LRC 8 ∧ LRC 9) from this statement, `mss_finite_checking` and `rosenfeld_eight_runners` (for LRC 7); the Lean proof of the gcd-normalisation (divide by g = gcd S) and the case split is complete.

title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 113 — on a theme by Dirac and Motzkin: the Kelly–Moser bound on ordinary lines
author: @Secousses
source:
Parent (mathematical): the Dirac-Motzkin conjecture on ordinary lines (at least n/2 ordinary lines for n points not all collinear, n large); no entry found on the platform by keyword search (the platform has the Sylvester-Gallai theorem itself, ProofsInTheBook.Chapter10.euclidean_sylvester_gallai, Proved). This statement is the Kelly-Moser partial result.
Source (verified by search): L. M. Kelly and W. O. J. Moser, 'On the number of ordinary lines determined by n points', Canad. J. Math. 10 (1958), 210-219 (bound 3n/7, sharp for n = 7 and 8). Context: Csima and Sawyer improved the constant to 6n/13 for n > 7 (year cited from memory); B. Green and T. Tao, 'On sets defining few ordinary lines', Discrete Comput. Geom. 50 (2013), 409-468 (verified).
Boundary check (exact integer arithmetic): the 7 points (0,0),(6,0),(0,6),(3,0),(0,3),(3,3),(2,2) (triangle, side midpoints, centroid) have exactly 3 ordinary lines, so 3n/7 = 3 is attained; 20000 random small integer sets gave no violation.

source:

Makai with ES(5) = 9; the first complete published proof is by Kalbfleisch, Kalbfleisch and Stanton (1970) (title, venue and pages cited from memory: 'A combinatorial problem on convex n-gons', Proc. Louisiana Conf. Combinatorics, Graph Theory and Computing, 180-188). ES(6) = 17 by Szekeres and Peters (2006, computer search; ANZIAM J. 48, verified). The Suk bound 2^(n+o(n)) (J. Amer. Math. Soc. 30 (2017)) is cited from memory.
